lessons.title: Sketch it before you code it
lessons.hook: Get the boxes right on paper, and the class file basically writes itself.

blocks.heading: Sketch the classes before you code
blocks.body: Before you open an editor, sketch the classes on paper first. That sketch has a standard notation, UML: one box per class, its fields listed inside, lines connecting boxes that need each other. A line between two boxes means one class holds a reference to the other — a has-a relationship, called an association. An open arrow from a smaller box up to a bigger one means the smaller class inherits everything the bigger one has — an is-a relationship. Decide which kind each connection is first. Then coding becomes translation, not invention: each box becomes a class, each listed field becomes a class field, and each line becomes either a stored reference or an extends clause.

blocks.caption: Static example, no Run button here. Square is-a Shape (extends). Drawing has-a Shape (a stored field). Same two relationships, side by side.

steps.say: Fields here are exactly the attributes the sketch listed — nothing invented while coding.
This extends mirrors the inheritance arrow directly — every field and method Vehicle has, Car now gets.
One class holding a reference to another class is what an association line meant on paper.
The constructor sets up that association once, so every method afterward can rely on it existing.
Calling vehicle.costFor(days) proves the association works — Rental leans on Vehicle instead of repeating its math.

blocks.caption: Every box from the sketch becomes a class; every connecting line becomes a field or an extends clause.

blocks.prompt: A Team class keeps a list of Player objects it manages. A Goalkeeper class extends Player and adds nothing else. Which pair of words correctly labels the two relationships?
options: Team has-a Player; Goalkeeper is-a Player
Team is-a Player; Goalkeeper has-a Player
Team has-a Player; Goalkeeper has-a Player
Team is-a Player; Goalkeeper is-a Player
why: Right — a stored list is a reference, so that is has-a, and extends is inheritance, so that is is-a.
Backwards — a stored list is an association, not inheritance, and extends is inheritance, not an association.
Team is right, but extends always means is-a, never has-a, no matter what the subclass adds.
A stored list is never inheritance — Team only holds Player objects, it does not extend Player.
blocks.hint: Look at what each relationship actually does: does one class extend the other, or just keep a reference to it?
blocks.explain: Team stores a list of Player references, so that is has-a — an association. Goalkeeper extends Player, so that is is-a — inheritance. Same two relationship types as the sketch, applied to a new pair of classes.

blocks.prompt: Finish Dog so a dog prints "Rex barks" while any other animal still prints "Milo makes a sound" — using a constructor and an override, not a new field. Main already reads the kind and the name for you.
blocks.hint: Give Dog a constructor that calls super(name), then override speak() to return something different from Animal's version.
blocks.explain: Dog's constructor passes name up with super(name), and overriding speak() lets the same call, a.speak(), produce a different result depending on the actual object — exactly what an is-a relationship promises.

bullets: Boxes on paper become classes; fields on paper become fields.
A stored reference is has-a; extends is is-a.
Code should mirror the sketch exactly, not improve on it while typing.
blocks.remember: Design the relationships first — has-a or is-a — then let the code follow.

blocks.say: Next you sketch a structure yourself, then build it in code without drifting from that sketch.

lessons.exitLine: Go sketch the next one first — then make the code match it exactly.
